papers.title: When Do Supervised UQ Ensembles Improve LLM Hallucination Detection? A Robustness Study
papers.abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods are widely used for hallucination detection in large language models (LLMs) in closed-book settings where ground-truth evidence is unavailable at inference time. Prior work has proposed combining UQ signals via learned ensembles, but empirical investigations into the robustness of these ensembles are limited. We study a supervised ensembling framework that trains a classifier over heterogeneous UQ-based scorer outputs on a small, domain-specific dataset of labeled LLM responses, then applies it to out-of-sample hallucination classification without retrieval, tools, or reference documents. Across four LLMs, nine datasets, and three generation regimes (short-form QA, long-form generation, and code generation), we provide a systematic robustness analysis along three axes: sample efficiency, in-domain dataset transfer, and generation regime dependence. We find that supervised ensembles outperform the best individual scorer in 30 of 32 settings, with gains realized from as few as 100 labeled instances. Ensembles retain most of their advantage in cases of in-domain transfer under distribution shift, outperforming the best non-ensemble scorer in 23 of 28 transfer settings. Sampling-based black-box ensembles are nearly as effective as full ensembles, while single-generation white-box ensembles offer limited benefit.

summary.takeaway: Supervised ensembles of heterogeneous UQ scorers consistently improve hallucination detection across LLMs and tasks, even with minimal labeled data.
summary.problem: Detecting hallucinations in closed‑book LLM outputs without external references.
summary.method: Train a classifier on a small domain‑specific set of UQ scorer outputs (black‑box, white‑box, reflexive) and apply it to out‑of‑sample detection.
summary.evidence: Ensembles beat the best individual scorer in 30 of 32 settings by AUROC, achieving gains with as few as 100 labeled examples.
summary.limitations: Study limited to four closed‑weight LLMs, three generation regimes, and narrow domains; open‑weight models and cross‑domain transfer remain untested.
summary.why_for_you: Matches your interest in trustworthy LLMs by providing a data‑efficient way to enhance hallucination detection.

signals.text: Supervised UQ ensembles outperform the best individual scorer in 30 of 32 settings, with AUROC gains from 100 labeled instances.
Ensemble trains a classifier (logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting) over 30+ heterogeneous UQ scores spanning black‑box, white‑box, and reflexive families.
Black‑box‑only ensembles match full ensembles, while white‑box‑only ensembles provide limited benefit; results may not generalize beyond four closed‑weight LLMs.

deep_dive.overview: The paper evaluates a supervised ensembling framework that learns to combine diverse uncertainty quantification (UQ) signals for hallucination detection in closed‑book LLM generation. Across four LLMs, nine datasets, and three generation regimes (short‑form QA, long‑form, code), the authors assess sample efficiency, in‑domain transfer, and regime dependence. Ensembles consistently surpass the strongest single scorer, achieving notable gains with as few as 100 labeled examples, and retain most of their advantage under distribution shift. Black‑box‑only ensembles are nearly as effective as full ensembles, whereas white‑box‑only ensembles add little value.

methodology.title: Supervised ensembling pipeline
methodology.detail: Collect K UQ scorer outputs per response, forming a vector in [0,1]^K; train a binary classifier on a small labeled set to predict hallucination (h(y)∈{0,1}).

methodology.title: Combination strategies
methodology.detail: Evaluate logistic regression, random forest, and gradient boosting classifiers, as well as weighted‑average baselines.

mechanism.title: Complementary UQ signals
mechanism.detail: Black‑box consistency, white‑box token probabilities, and reflexive self‑confidence provide orthogonal evidence of correctness, enabling the classifier to learn task‑specific weighting.

mechanism.title: Supervised weighting
mechanism.detail: The classifier learns to emphasize the most predictive scorers for each domain and generation regime, overcoming brittle zero‑shot thresholds.

experiments.title: Model and dataset coverage
experiments.detail: Four LLMs (Gemini‑2.5‑Flash, Gemini‑2.5‑Pro, GPT‑4o, GPT‑4o‑mini) evaluated on nine benchmarks: Math (OpenR1‑Math, BigMath), Factual QA (HotpotQA, SimpleQA), Reading Comprehension (DROP), Code (LiveCodeBench Python subsets), Long‑form (rivers, mushrooms).

experiments.title: Training regimes
experiments.detail: Subsample training folds at 0.1N–0.7N (N = dataset size); evaluate AUROC and Expected Calibration Error (ECE) across 25 stratified 70/30 splits.

experiments.title: Baselines and metrics
experiments.detail: Best individual scorer (optimistic test‑set selection) serves as baseline; report mean AUROC with 95% CI and ECE for each setting.

findings.title: Overall performance gain
findings.detail: Ensembles outperform the best individual scorer in 30/32 settings by AUROC and 29/32 by ECE.

findings.title: Sample efficiency
findings.detail: Statistically significant AUROC improvements appear with as few as 100 labeled instances.

findings.title: In‑domain transfer
findings.detail: Under distribution shift, ensembles remain superior in 23/28 transfer settings.

findings.title: Black‑box vs. full ensembles
findings.detail: Sampling‑based black‑box ensembles achieve near‑parity with full ensembles; white‑box‑only ensembles show limited benefit.

contributions: Systematic robustness analysis of supervised UQ ensembles across sample efficiency, in‑domain transfer, and generation regime dimensions.
limitations: Evaluation limited to four closed‑weight LLMs from two providers; open‑weight models and internal‑state scorers are not examined.
Domain coverage restricted to specific math, factual QA, Python code, and two narrow long‑form factoid tasks; broader tasks and cross‑domain/LLM transfer are untested.
open_questions: How do supervised UQ ensembles perform with open‑weight models that expose hidden representations?
Can ensembles trained on one generation regime (e.g., short‑form QA) transfer effectively to a different regime (e.g., multi‑turn dialogue)?
What is the trade‑off between ensemble inference cost and detection accuracy in real‑time deployment?

papers.title: Across the Loss Landscape with Progressive Growth
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks generalize well despite their highly nonconvex, overparameterized loss landscapes, a phenomenon often associated with the geometry of the minima found by stochastic optimization. We study how incremental grow-and-optimize strategies bias training toward flatter regions by viewing growth as progressive constraint relaxation. Starting from a low-dimensional submodel, we iteratively expand the trainable parameters by unlocking nested random subspaces while freezing the orthogonal complement at the network initialization, re-optimizing after each expansion until the full architecture is reached. Under standard local regularity conditions around non-degenerate minima, we prove that local sublevel sets are well approximated by ellipsoids and that basin accessibility under frozen constraints can be characterized by an explicit effective curvature in the frozen directions. This leads to an explanation of the bias: progressive growth increases the relative weight of wide basins and suppresses sharp ones through a volume effect induced by the frozen constraints. We empirically validate these predictions in controlled toy landscapes and in a realistic ResNet/CIFAR-100 setting and confirm that although progressive subspace growth reliably produces flatter solutions, curvature reductions do not universally translate into improved test performance, highlighting subtleties in the flatness-generalization connection. The code is available at https://github.com/p0lcAi/Across-the-Loss-Landscape.

papers.title: On-policy Distillation with Verifiable Reward
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) and on-policy distillation (OPD) have become two widely adopted paradigms for post-training large language models. However, RLVR suffers from sparse task-level feedback, while OPD provides dense token-level guidance but ignores trajectory correctness, limiting its performance to that of the teacher. Combining them is a promising direction: OPD supplies dense supervisory signals, while RLVR provides task-level correctness. Nevertheless, existing integrations often rely on weighted combination or heuristic switching, introducing extra hyperparameters and trade-offs. We propose On-policy Distillation with Verifiable Reward (OPDVR), a simple yet effective method that seamlessly combines OPD and RLVR without adding any hyperparameters. We first reformulate the implicit reward of sampled-token OPD based on trajectory correctness, then apply a ReLU gating mechanism to ensure that correct trajectories receive non-negative rewards and incorrect ones receive non-positive rewards---thereby aligning the distillation signal with task success while preserving the teacher's distributional guidance. Furthermore, our modification transforms sampled-token OPD into a proper RLVR method, making it readily combinable with any policy gradient algorithm, such as GRPO. Experiments on six reasoning benchmarks show that OPDVR consistently outperforms standard OPD. Our code is available at https://github.com/LeapLabTHU/OPDVR.

summary.limitations: 评估仅限于数学推理基准和单一学生‑教师配对。
summary.evidence: 在六个推理基准上，OPDVR 的平均准确率为 49.1%，而标准 OPD 为 42.0%，逆向门控变体表现更差。
summary.method: OPDVR 重新表述采样‑token OPD 奖励，并使用 ReLU 门控，使正确轨迹的奖励非负，错误轨迹的奖励非正。
summary.problem: RLVR 提供稀疏的任务级奖励，而 OPD 给出密集的 token 引导但忽视轨迹正确性，限制了学生模型的表现。
summary.why_for_you: 鉴于您关注 on‑policy 蒸馏，OPDVR 提供一种无需超参数的方式，在可验证奖励下提升 OPD。
summary.takeaway: OPDVR 在 on‑policy 蒸馏中加入简单的 ReLU 门，使其成为可验证奖励方法，并在推理性能上提升且无需额外超参数。

experiments.title: 基准评估
experiments.detail: 学生模型 Qwen3‑4B 从教师 Qwen3‑4B‑RL 蒸馏；六个推理基准 (AIME24, AIME25, AMC, MATH500, Minerva, OlympiadBench) 使用 avg@16 准确率衡量；基线：标准 OPD 与逆向门控变体；硬件：NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 GPU。

deep_dive.overview: 本文指出采样‑token on‑policy 蒸馏 (OPD) 与可验证奖励强化学习 (RLVR) 之间的不匹配：OPD 的 token 级优势可能与轨迹正确性冲突。OPDVR 通过重新表述 OPD 奖励并加入 ReLU 门，使 token 优势与验证器的二元奖励对齐，从而消除有害的梯度成分。该修改无需额外超参数，可与任意策略梯度算法结合。六个数学推理数据集的实验显示，相比普通 OPD 均有一致提升，验证了门控机制的有效性。

methodology.title: 奖励重构
methodology.detail: 采样‑token OPD 可表示为二元任务奖励 (+1 或 –1) 乘以教师‑学生对数概率比，暴露出符号不一致的无界问题。

methodology.title: ReLU 门控机制
methodology.detail: 对验证器奖励 R 与 token‑级优势 rt 的乘积使用 ReLU，得到 reward = ReLU(R·rt)；这迫使正确轨迹的 token 奖励为非负，错误轨迹为非正。

methodology.title: 与策略梯度的集成
methodology.detail: 门控奖励可直接嵌入标准策略梯度更新（如 GRPO），使 OPDVR 能作为 OPD 的即插即用替代，无需额外的损失加权。

limitations: 仅在数学推理基准上评估，缺乏对其他任务的通用性证据
未对计算开销或训练稳定性进行分析，除已报告的曲线外缺乏进一步评估

findings.title: 性能提升
findings.detail: OPDVR 的平均准确率为 49.1%，而 OPD 为 42.0%；逆向门控变体低于 OPD，证实门控的必要性。

contributions: 通过 ReLU 门实现 OPD 与 RLVR 的无超参数组合
理论分析表明 OPDVR 消除与验证器冲突的梯度成分
在六个数学推理基准上进行实证验证
open_questions: OPDVR 在非推理或多模态任务上的表现如何？
门控机制能否适配二元正确性以外的奖励结构？
OPDVR 对训练效率和大模型可扩展性的影响是什么？

mechanism.title: 冲突消除
mechanism.detail: 门控更新将原始 OPD 梯度分解为无冲突分量 (ΔOPDVR) 与冲突项，后者在投影到验证器梯度上时为非正，确保与可验证奖励对齐。

signals.text: OPDVR 引入无超参数的 ReLU 门，将采样‑token OPD 转换为合规的 RLVR 方法。
该门控通过对验证信号与 token‑级优势的乘积使用 ReLU，强制正确轨迹的 token 奖励为非负，错误轨迹为非正。
OPDVR 在六个推理基准上实现 49.1% 的平均准确率，优于 OPD 的 42.0%，并超越逆向门控变体。

papers.title: Constrained Entity Selection under Partial Knowledge for LLM-Based Knowledge Graph QA
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for knowledge graph question answering (KGQA), but can fail to correctly ground answers in the underlying graph. Current approaches to LLM-based KGQA either rely on full semantic parsing into executable queries such as SPARQL, which is brittle in practice due to complex schemas or incompleteness of real-world KGs, or on LLM-reasoning and answer generation over KGs, which can be more robust but lacks formal guarantees. In this work, we study a complementary setting in which \emph{candidate} answers are generated by an LLM-based system and subsequently verified using lightweight symbolic constraints derived from the question. We introduce \emph{Constrained Entity Selection under Partial Knowledge (CES-PK)}, a problem formulation that focuses on eliminating invalid answers and providing symbolic support for valid ones without requiring construction of executable logical forms. To account for incomplete KGs, we employ a three-valued constraint semantics (\emph{satisfied, violated, unknown}) that avoids incorrect rejections under open-world assumptions. To demonstrate the effects of our method, we instantiate this framework over the Hetionet biomedical knowledge graph and evaluate the impact of type, relation, and exclusion constraints. Experiments show that precision improves by filtering invalid candidates, while recall is preserved due to retaining candidates whose constraints are not explicitly violated. Satisfied constraints provide additional positive symbolic evidence to rank remaining candidates.
papers.comment: 8 pages, 2 tables. Submitted manuscript. Revised version published in KI 2026: Advances in Artificial Intelligence, LNCS 16830

summary.takeaway: Lightweight constraint verification can substantially raise precision of LLM‑generated KGQA answers while keeping recall intact.
summary.problem: LLM‑based KGQA often produces answers that are not grounded in the underlying knowledge graph, especially when the graph is incomplete.
summary.method: The paper proposes post‑hoc verification using extracted type, relation, and exclusion constraints evaluated with a three‑valued semantics.
summary.evidence: Precision improves from 0.41 to 0.66 overall (Q2 precision jumps from 0.17 to 0.62) with recall unchanged at 1.0 on Hetionet.
summary.limitations: Evaluation relies on simulated candidate sets and assumes the KG is factually correct but incomplete.
summary.why_for_you: Provides a symbolic, efficient filtering layer that aligns with interests in robust, low‑overhead methods for LLM output verification.

signals.text: Introduces CES-PK, a post‑hoc verification formulation that eliminates invalid LLM answers without full logical forms.
Applies three‑valued constraint semantics (satisfied, violated, unknown) to filter candidates and assign support scores.
Achieves precision rise from 0.41 to 0.66 (Q2 up to 0.62) with unchanged recall, on simulated data.

deep_dive.overview: The authors address the grounding gap in LLM‑driven KGQA by introducing Constrained Entity Selection under Partial Knowledge (CES‑PK), a verification stage that uses lightweight constraints derived from the question. Constraints are evaluated with a three‑valued semantics to either discard clearly invalid candidates or award positive support when satisfied, preserving recall under open‑world assumptions. Experiments on the Hetionet biomedical KG with two query templates show notable precision gains, especially when exclusion constraints are present, while recall remains perfect. Limitations stem from the controlled simulation setting and reliance on a correct but incomplete KG.

methodology.title: Constraint extraction
methodology.detail: From each natural‑language question, the system derives type constraints (C1), positive relation constraints (C2), and exclusion constraints (C3) that are necessary for a correct answer.

methodology.title: Three‑valued semantics evaluation
methodology.detail: Each constraint is classified as satisfied, violated, or unknown based on the KG; violations trigger candidate removal, satisfied constraints contribute a support score, and unknowns are ignored.

mechanism.title: Filtering vs. support
mechanism.detail: Violations (negative signal) cause hard filtering, while satisfied constraints (positive signal) increase a candidate's support value used for ranking.

mechanism.title: Open‑world handling
mechanism.detail: The unknown category prevents false negatives when KG edges are missing, ensuring recall is not harmed.

experiments.title: Controlled Hetionet study
experiments.detail: Using the Hetionet biomedical KG, two query types (Q1: compounds treating disease; Q2: compounds treating disease but not causing side effect) were sampled. Gold answer sets were combined with distractors to simulate LLM output. Metrics: precision before/after filtering, recall (always 1.0), and mean support for gold vs. non‑gold candidates.

experiments.title: KG incompleteness analysis
experiments.detail: A second experiment removed 10 % of relevant edges, measuring the drop in precision and support while confirming recall stability.

findings.title: Precision gains
findings.detail: Overall precision rose from 0.41 to 0.66; Q2 precision increased by +0.45 (0.17 → 0.62) due to exclusion constraints.

findings.title: Constraint role differentiation
findings.detail: Type constraints consistently filter type‑incorrect candidates; exclusion constraints provide the strongest negative signal; relation constraints rarely cause violations but boost support for gold answers.

findings.title: Impact of incompleteness
findings.detail: Removing 10 % of edges lowered post‑filter precision (e.g., Q1 to 0.70) and support scores, yet recall remained at 1.0.

contributions: Formulation of CES‑PK for post‑hoc verification without full semantic parsing
Three‑valued constraint semantics to handle incomplete knowledge graphs
Empirical demonstration of precision improvement on a biomedical KG
limitations: Evaluation uses simulated candidate sets rather than a full end‑to‑end KGQA pipeline
Assumes the underlying KG is factually correct; noisy or erroneous triples could cause false rejections
All candidate entities are presumed present in the KG
open_questions: How does CES‑PK integrate with real‑world LLM‑based KGQA systems and affect overall end‑to‑end performance?
Can constraint extraction be automated for more complex query structures and larger schema vocabularies?
What is the robustness of the three‑valued semantics when the KG contains systematic noise or contradictory facts?

papers.title: A Dual-Dimensional LLM Framework for Automated Item Incidental Content Similarity Analysis in Large-Scale Assessments
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of large-scale assessments and the growing adoption of automatic item generation have intensified concerns about incidental content redundancy, where construct-irrelevant elements such as wording or contextual framing become unintentionally repetitive across items. Traditional similarity metrics like BLEU or cosine similarity, often fail to capture the nuanced structural and semantic layers that drive perceived redundancy simultaneously. This study proposes a dual-dimensional framework for Automated Item Similarity Analysis (AISA) powered by Large Language Models (LLMs), operationalizing similarity through Structured Decomposition and Semantic Relatedness. Psychometric validation indicates that LLM-derived metrics align more closely with indicators of construct-irrelevant local dependence and yield more coherent item parameter groupings than traditional text-based measures. The framework is further evaluated through its application in Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT). Simulations reveal that incorporating LLM-based similarity constraints into item selection improves estimation stability and reduces bias with minimal efficiency trade-offs, outperforming constraints based on conventional metrics. These findings highlight the potential of LLM-powered AISA to support scalable bank curation, content-aware test assembly, and experience-sensitive adaptive testing across diverse assessment contexts.

summary.takeaway: A dual‑dimensional LLM similarity framework better captures incidental item redundancy than traditional text metrics.
summary.problem: Incidental content redundancy in large item banks is poorly detected by existing lexical or embedding similarity measures.
summary.method: The authors prompt LLMs to output separate structural and semantic similarity scores for item pairs and use these in psychometric clustering and CAT constraints.
summary.evidence: Empirical results show moderate correlation between dimensions (r=0.66), weak alignment with BLEU (r=0.30) and cosine (r=0.43), and CAT simulations that reduce bias and improve estimation stability with minimal efficiency loss.
summary.limitations: Authors do not report real‑world deployment or runtime costs, and no explicit limitation is stated.
summary.why_for_you: Relevant if you study LLM loss landscapes affecting multi‑dimensional similarity scoring mechanisms.

signals.text: Introduces a dual‑dimensional LLM framework (structured decomposition + semantic relatedness) for incidental item similarity.
Uses LLM prompts to produce separate structural and semantic similarity scores, then clusters items for CAT constraints.
Reports r=0.66 between dimensions, BLEU r=0.30, cosine r=0.43, and CAT simulations improve stability with minimal efficiency loss.

deep_dive.overview: The paper presents AISA, a dual‑dimensional framework that leverages large language models to quantify incidental item similarity along structural and semantic axes. Structured prompts elicit separate similarity scores, which are then used to form psychometrically coherent clusters and to impose content‑diversity constraints in computerized adaptive testing. Validation shows the scores capture information beyond BLEU and cosine similarity, aligning with construct‑irrelevant local dependence, and simulations demonstrate improved estimation stability and reduced bias with negligible efficiency trade‑offs.

methodology.title: Structured Decomposition Prompt
methodology.detail: A prompt asks the LLM to assess surface‑level structural similarity (e.g., scenario, phrasing) between two items, returning a normalized score.

methodology.title: Semantic Relatedness Prompt
methodology.detail: A separate prompt requests the LLM to evaluate deeper semantic coherence (logical flow, meaning) between the same item pair, also yielding a normalized score.

mechanism.title: Dual‑dimensional Scoring
mechanism.detail: The two scores are treated as orthogonal dimensions (correlation r=0.66) to represent incidental content more comprehensively than single‑metric approaches.

mechanism.title: Cluster‑constrained Item Selection
mechanism.detail: Items are clustered based on combined scores; during CAT, selection is restricted to maintain cluster diversity, reducing local dependence.

experiments.title: Psychometric Correlation Study
experiments.detail: Computed Pearson correlations between LLM scores and traditional metrics (BLEU r=0.30, cosine r=0.43) and with residual correlations indicating construct‑irrelevant local dependence.

experiments.title: Clustering Evaluation
experiments.detail: Compared item clusters derived from LLM scores versus BLEU/cosine clusters on discrimination and threshold parameter coherence.

experiments.title: CAT Simulation
experiments.detail: Simulated adaptive testing with and without LLM‑based similarity constraints, measuring estimation stability, bias, and test length efficiency.

findings.title: Dimensional Alignment
findings.detail: Structural and semantic similarity scores show a moderate positive correlation (r=0.66), indicating related but distinct information.

findings.title: Added Information Over Traditional Metrics
findings.detail: LLM scores correlate weakly with BLEU and cosine, suggesting they capture additional aspects of incidental content.

findings.title: Psychometric Coherence
findings.detail: Clusters based on LLM scores exhibit clearer discrimination and threshold structures than those based on BLEU or cosine.

findings.title: CAT Performance Gains

papers.title: A Judge Should Know What Changed:Construct Validity for LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation
papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation is usually assessed by agreement and robustness to surface perturbations, but reliability does not establish construct validity. We formalize construct validity for an evaluator as a two-dimensional profile: invariance S, the probability that a verdict is unchanged under construct-preserving edits, and construct sensitivity R, the probability that it changes under minimal construct-changing edits. We show that S and R are independent and that no scalar summary preserves all relevant comparisons. We measure the profile across 7 judges and 4 domains using 7 construct-changing intervention types and 5 register-only controls, with intervention direction determined by human annotators and generation, verification, and judging assigned to disjoint model families. At matched invariance S >= 0.90, judges average S = 0.945 but R = 0.319. Sensitivity also differs between scope and strength edits: R_scope = 0.383 versus R_strength = 0.262, a +0.121 gap with the same sign for all 7 judges. We further audit five public label sets and find that surface-only predictors reproduce 55%-67% of labels in paired mode, including 67.4% of MT-Bench human votes. These results show that high judge agreement can coexist with weak sensitivity to changes in the construct being evaluated, motivating joint reporting of invariance and sensitivity and auditing the validation set itself.

summary.evidence: 在S≥0.90条件下，裁判平均S=0.945但R=0.319，不同编辑类型敏感性差异达+0.121，表面预测器可复现55%-67%标签
summary.limitations: 未提及具体方法局限性，仅说明单一标量无法完整表征比较
summary.method: 定义S为构念保持编辑下的判决不变概率，R为最小构念改变编辑下的判决变化概率，通过7个裁判和4个领域实验测量双维指标
summary.problem: 现有LLM评估方法仅关注一致性与鲁棒性，未验证评估过程是否真正捕捉目标构念
summary.takeaway: 提出LLM-as-a-judge评估的构念效度双维指标S（不变性）和R（构念敏感性），证明其独立性并揭示高一致率下敏感性不足的矛盾现象
summary.why_for_you: 构念效度验证直接关联LLM可信性评估，双维指标为对抗训练中的鲁棒性与敏感性平衡提供新视角
